papers.title: Distinct handwriting kinematic profiles across Parkinson's disease subtypes.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Handwriting impairment is common in Parkinson's disease (PD), but its relationships with clinical severity and motor phenotypes remain incompletely understood. AIM: To characterize handwriting kinematics in PD and examine their associations with clinical severity and motor phenotypes. METHODS: Fifty-six patients with PD and 46 healthy controls (HC) performed a standardized digital handwriting task in the medication OFF state. Letter area, duration, pressure, writing speed, and the progressive micrographia (PM) index were analyzed. TD and AR subtypes were compared, and correlation and ROC analyses were performed. RESULTS: PD patients showed significant handwriting abnormalities compared with HC. Using a >30% reduction in mean letter area to define categorical progressive micrographia, PM was observed in 8.9% of patients with PD and 2.2% of healthy controls (p = 0.219). The continuous PM index and twenty-letter duration showed discriminative performance, with AUCs of 0.753 and 0.718, respectively (both p < 0.001). Compared with TD patients, AR patients exhibited smaller writing areas (initial five-letter area, p = 0.042; twenty-letter area, p = 0.013; final five-letter area, p = 0.024) and slower writing speed (p = 0.012). Twenty-letter duration correlated with HY stage (r = 0.290, p = 0.030) and MDS-UPDRS-III scores (r = 0.404, p = 0.006). Overall, temporal parameters, particularly letter duration, were more closely associated with disease severity, whereas spatial measures showed weaker clinical correlations despite clear between-group differences. CONCLUSION: Temporal measures were more closely associated with clinical severity, whereas spatial measures showed weaker and less consistent associations. papers.title: Depression in the prodromal phase of Parkinson's disease: Clinical manifestations, biomarker evidence, and predictive implications.
papers.abstract: Depression is one of the earliest and most frequent non-motor symptoms in the prodromal phase of Parkinson's disease (PD), often preceding motor signs by years to decades. This review synthesizes epidemiological, neuroimaging, biomarker, and genetic evidence to clarify whether depression is a risk factor, a direct prodromal manifestation, or both. Meta-analyses consistently show a two-fold increased risk of subsequent PD in individuals with depressive symptoms or major depressive disorder (MDD), with the highest risk occurring within 1-2 years of diagnosis but persisting for up to 25 years. Late-onset depressive syndrome (after age 50-60) is associated with dopaminergic deficits on dopamine transporter imaging in 24-79% of cases, supporting it as a prodromal symptom, whereas early-onset depression may act through shared genetic vulnerability or chronic inflammatory pathways. Neuroimaging in isolated REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD) reveals that depression correlates with caudate atrophy, frontostriatal white matter disruption, and brainstem monoaminergic dysfunction, but not simply with nigrostriatal denervation. Depression frequently coexists with RBD, autonomic dysfunction, and olfactory impairment, likely reflecting shared brainstem pathology. Genetic forms of PD (GBA1, SNCA, LRRK2, PRKN) show variable depression prevalence, providing mechanistic insights into lysosomal, inflammatory, and proteostatic pathways. Emerging evidence implicates IL-17A, sIL-2R, and α-synuclein (α-syn) aggregation as convergent points linking depression and prodromal α-synucleinopathy, with gut-brain axis dysfunction potentially amplifying this process. Current Movement Disorder Society prodromal PD criteria include depression but have limited sensitivity in general populations. No disease-modifying trials have tested whether treating prodromal depression alters phenoconversion risk. We conclude that proximal, late-onset depressive syndrome is a robust prodromal mark

papers.title: Hierarchical deep learning-radiomics fusion for differentiating Parkinson's disease from atypical Parkinsonism using FP-CIT imaging.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) and atypical Parkinsonism (AP) are challenging to differentiate, particularly in the early stages, because of overlapping motor symptoms and similar dopaminergic neurodegenerative patterns. We developed an interpretable artificial intelligence (AI) framework integrating deep learning and radiomics using automatically extracted striatal regions of interest (ROIs) from FP-CIT imaging for the differential diagnosis of Parkinsonian disorders. METHODS: A total of 228 participants, including healthy controls (HC), patients with PD, and patients with AP, were retrospectively analyzed. Striatal ROIs were automatically extracted from FP-CIT images using a hotspot-based bounding-box algorithm. Radiomics features and deep learning-derived imaging features were integrated using a hierarchical late fusion framework. Hierarchical classification was performed in two stages: HC versus Parkinsonism, followed by PD versus AP. Model interpretability was evaluated using Grad-CAM and SHAP analyses. RESULTS: Across five random seeds, the validation-selected late-fusion model achieved a mean held-out test accuracy, F1-score, and ROC-AUC of 0.906, 0.942, and 0.969, respectively, for Stage 1 (HC vs. parkinsonism) and 0.815, 0.669, and 0.880 for Stage 2 (PD vs. AP). The ablation analysis showed modest improvements in mean accuracy and F1-score over the deep learning-only model in both stages. Grad-CAM provided qualitative visualizations of the image regions contributing to model predictions, while SHAP identified stage-dependent radiomics importance profiles primarily involving voxel-intensity distributions and texture heterogeneity. CONCLUSION: The proposed framework demonstrated promising internal performance for the hierarchical classification of Parkinsonian disorders and provided exploratory information regarding the image regions and radiomics features contributing to model predictions. papers.title: Management of fragile X-associated tremor ataxia syndrome: a review for clinicians.
papers.abstract: Fragile X-associated tremor ataxia syndrome (FXTAS) is a multi-faceted and progressive neurodegenerative disorder that manifests clinically with action tremor, gait ataxia, parkinsonism, peripheral neuropathy, and cognitive and psychiatric features. The disease is highly heterogeneous and there are no FDA approved medications for FXTAS as a specific indication. As such, treatment is symptomatic and must be tailored to the specific needs of a given patient. This review provides expert opinion-based treatment recommendations for the core and ancillary clinical features of FXTAS. Movement disorders, such as tremor, ataxia and parkinsonism may respond to symptomatic medications and therapies, but caution is required when considering surgical interventions such as deep brain stimulation. Cognitive decline can be responsive to medications developed for other cognitive disorders, but these medications work best when combined with non-medication based approaches and all patients should be screened for other reversible causes of memory decline. Psychiatric symptoms, including anxiety, depression, and psychosis, can be treated with psychotherapy and medications; but caution is required to avoid exacerbating clinical and subclinical movement disorder features with psychotropic medications. Rehabilitative therapies, such as speech therapy, occupational, and physical therapy, often enhance patient function and quality of life. Exercise and good nutrition are recommendations that are common to other cerebellar ataxias and adult neurodegenerative disorders and may have a positive impact on general health. A multi-disciplinary approach is recommended to address all components of FXTAS.

papers.title: Hierarchical reorganization of cortical and cerebellar functional gradients in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a common movement disorder with heterogeneous clinical manifestations, and its tremor-predominant presentations may overlap with essential tremor (ET), complicating clinical differentiation in some patients. Functional gradient analysis provides a continuous framework for characterizing macroscale brain hierarchical organization and may offer candidate imaging features for disease characterization. METHODS: We first investigated surface-based resting-state functional measures and cerebral perfusion in 50 patients with idiopathic PD and 33 healthy controls. We subsequently incorporated functional MRI data from 17 patients with ET to examine alterations in cortical and cerebellar functional gradients in PD and ET and to evaluate their potential utility for distinguishing the two disorders. Group comparisons, gradient range and variance analyses, network-level analyses, and multiclass support vector machine classification were performed. RESULTS: Patients with PD showed widespread abnormalities in both cortical and cerebellar Gradient 1 and Gradient 2, whereas patients with ET exhibited fewer cortical alterations and no significant cerebellar gradient abnormalities. At the group level, both PD and ET showed broader cortical gradient ranges; however, only PD demonstrated significantly increased individual-level gradient range and variance. Network-level analyses further revealed pronounced hierarchical redistribution between sensorimotor and higher-order associative systems in PD, while ET displayed relatively limited alterations. The combined use of cortical and cerebellar Gradient 1 and Gradient 2 features showed discriminatory performance within the present dataset, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values of 1.000 for healthy controls, 0.960 for PD, and 0.889 for ET. papers.title: Comparative effects and dose-response relationships of exercise for finger dexterity and upper-limb function in Parkinson's disease: a Bayesian network and model-based dose-response meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Upper-limb impairment limits independence in Parkinson's disease (PD), but the comparative effects and dose-response profiles of exercise modalities remain uncertain. METHODS: PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL, Web of Science, Scopus, and SPORTDiscus were searched from inception to June 20, 2026. Studies that qualified were randomized controlled trials of structured exercise or rehabilitation in adults with PD. Bayesian random-effects network meta-analysis and model-based dose-response network meta-analysis were conducted separately for finger dexterity and upper-limb function. Weekly dose was expressed as metabolic equivalent of task minutes per week (MET·min/week), and evidence certainty was assessed using CINeMA. RESULTS: Thirty-six reports comprising 1,575 participants were included. Aerobic exercise training (Hedges' g CONCLUSION: Exercise effects were outcome specific. The findings can inform exercise-modality selection and future dose-ranging trials, but they do not establish an optimal dose or justify a uniform clinical prescription. papers.title: Discovery of benzoxazole derivatives as novel α-synuclein aggregate ligands with potential for PET tracer development.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder worldwide, and the abnormal aggregation of α-synuclein (α-Syn) constitutes its core pathological hallmark. Positron emission tomography (PET) imaging of cerebral α-Syn aggregates holds great promise for the early diagnosis of PD. However, the imaging quality critically depends on the ligands with high binding affinity and selectivity for α-Syn aggregates. papers.title: Coexistence of anhedonia and sensation-seeking with context-dependent gut dysbiosis in a prodromal transgenic mouse model of Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Accumulating evidence indicates that gut microbiota plays a role in the progression of Parkinson's disease (PD). Microbiota-based treatments for prodromal PD, which is accompanied by a wide range of neuropsychiatric symptoms, are being considered a potential early intervention but are still under-investigated. This study examined the association between symptoms of affective and motivational impairments and gut dysbiosis in a transgenic mouse model (line G2-3) that overexpresses A53T mutant α-synuclein, a key protein involved in the disease pathology. By introducing biologically meaningful variations, such as genotype-based social grouping, efforts have been made to strengthen validity of the results and their translational relevance. Behavioral assessment was conducted on 6-month-old mice (the premotor stage) using Open Field, Elevated Plus Maze, Sucrose Preference and Tail Suspension tests. Fecal microbiota of mice was analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Obtained data revealed a strong behavioral phenotype in transgenic mice expressed as co-occurrence of consummatory anhedonia and sensation-seeking/risk-taking behavior, without significant motivational deficits and with variable gut dysbiosis: mixed-genotype housing, among others, prominently favored Bacteroidaceae/Bacteroides, as observed in PD patients, while single-genotype housing increased Dubosiella, a key bacteria in gut-originated PD model, along with the enrichment of Bifidobacterium pseudolongum, a well-known health-promoting bacterium. Overall, using a mouse model with adequate construct validity, this study identifies challenges in novel strategies that consider gut microbiota as an early diagnostic and therapeutic target for PD; it highlights the potential of the examined transgenic strain in studying low hedonic tone- and sensation-seeking-associated PD prodrome, building the basis for personalized medicine.

papers.title: Linking protein misfolding and heat stress: a common role for the kynurenine pathway.
papers.abstract: The kynurenine pathway (KP) of tryptophan metabolism is emerging as a key regulator of immune response, neuroinflammation, and neurodegeneration. Tryptophan-derived metabolites influence multiple processes, including excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and protein aggregation, which are underlying mechanisms in major neurological disorders. Dysregulation of the KP leads to an imbalance between neuroactive metabolites such as kynurenic acid quinolinic acid and 3-hydroxykynurenine, contributing to neuronal dysfunction and disease progression. This imbalance is associated with chronic proteinopathies such as Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease, where persistent neuroinflammation and excitotoxicity sustain the activation of KP and subsequent neurodegeneration. Importantly, KP activation is not only limited to chronic conditions but may also occur in acute neurological insults such as heatstroke, where impaired thermoregulation contributes to systemic inflammatory responses, oxidative stress, and disruption of the blood-brain barrier. Consequently, this facilitates the influx of peripheral kynurenine into the brain and its conversion into neuroactive metabolites, linking peripheral immune activation and neuronal injury. These findings highlight KP as a mechanistic bridge between acute and chronic neuropathological processes. In addition, the KP involvement in NAD⁺ production links immune activation and cellular energy metabolism, subsequently increasing neuronal vulnerability, particularly under stress. Emerging evidence further supports the potential of KP metabolites as diagnostic biomarkers for disease progression and severity, as well as possible therapeutic targets. Targeting key enzymes within the KP may offer novel strategies to reduce neurotoxicity and restore metabolic balance, which subsequently improves clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Tristetraprolin attenuates microglial neuroinflammation via post-transcriptional destabilization of TRAF6 mRNA in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Microglia-driven neuroinflammation is a central pathological hallmark of Parkinson's disease. Tristetraprolin (TTP), an RNA-binding protein, suppresses inflammation through facilitating the degradation of target mRNAs. However, its specific role in microglial activation during Parkinson's pathogenesis remains poorly characterized. METHODS: Transcriptomic analysis was performed to identify the differentially expressed genes in A53T α-synuclein transgenic mice. TTP expression and function were assessed in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistic studies employed RNA immunoprecipitation, dual-luciferase reporter assays, and mRNA stability analyses. Therapeutic efficacy was evaluated using the NF-κB inhibitor dimethylamino parthenolide (DMAPT) in conjunction with behavioral assessments. RESULTS: Transcriptomic analysis revealed significant upregulation of TTP in A53T mice, accompanied by enrichment of neuroinflammatory pathways. Immunofluorescence analysis identified that increased TTP expression was mainly detected in IBA1-positive microglia. Functionally, TTP knockdown enhanced pro-inflammatory cytokine production and exacerbated primary neuronal apoptosis. Mechanistically, TTP directly bound to the 3'-untranslated region (3'UTR) of TRAF6 mRNA, accelerating its degradation and thereby suppressing TRAF6/NF-κB signaling. In vivo, TTP knockdown enhanced neuroinflammation and aggravated dopaminergic neuron loss. Pharmacological inhibition of NF-κB by DMAPT attenuated microglial activation, preserved dopaminergic neurons, and ameliorated behavioral deficits. CONCLUSIONS: TTP mitigated microglial neuroinflammation by promoting TRAF6 mRNA degradation and suppressing NF-κB signaling. Targeting NF-κB with DMAPT may represent a promising druggable strategy.

papers.title: The GBA1-related variant rs12411216 is Associated with Motor and Non-Motor Impairments and Unfavorable Progression in Parkinson's Disease: A Five-Year Longitudinal Study.
papers.abstract: We investigated four regulatory single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) related to genes previously implicated in the autophagy-lysosomal pathway (rs76904798 and rs6581622 (LRRK2), rs356182 (SNCA), and rs12411216 (GBA1)) in order to assess their association with the clinical heterogeneity of Parkinson's disease. In a five-year observational study, 518 patients stratified by genotype were analyzed for cognitive, neuropsychiatric, motor, and other clinical signs.The rs356182 (SNCA) variant showed a modest association with disease traits, including significant associations with anxiety (HAMILTON scale). Conversely, the regulatory GBA1-related variant rs12411216 demonstrated a robust pleiotropic association with earlier disease onset, more severe motor impairment, and a broad spectrum of non-motor impairments, including anxiety, depression, impulsive-compulsive behaviors, and cognitive deficits. Longitudinal analyses revealed that patients homozygous for the rs12411216 AA genotype exhibited the most unfavorable progression across multiple domains, suggesting a faster neurocognitive decline.These findings suggest that the distinct pleiotropic effects of the GBA1-related variant rs12411216 contribute significantly to the clinical heterogeneity of PD by shaping unfavorable motor and neuropsychiatric progression trajectories. While the longitudinal design provides new evidence for genotype-dependent patterns, further functional studies are needed to confirm the proposed mechanistic link.

papers.title: Dual Health and Economic Burden of Multimorbidity in Aging Populations.
papers.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Population aging is contributing to rising multimorbidity across physical, psychological, and cognitive domains, yet global evidence integrating health and economic burdens in older adults remains limited. OBJECTIVES: To quantify the global health and economic burden of multimorbidity among adults aged 60 years or older and to assess trends from 2000 to 2023. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This economic evaluation used observational modeling of Global Burden of Disease study 2023 estimates as health inputs and integrated them with macroeconomic, health expenditure, and population data from World Bank Open Data, the World Health Organization Global Health Expenditure Database, and United Nations population data. Health burden analyses covered adults aged 60 years or older in 204 countries and territories from 2000 to 2023, and economic burden analyses covered 180 countries and territories. Data analyses were performed from January 27 to July 22, 2026. EXPOSURES: Cross-domain multimorbidity spanning physical conditions, psychological disorders, and cognitive disorders, operationalized as 78 multimorbidity combinations. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The main outcomes were years lived with disability (YLDs) per 100 000 population and economic losses. All economic indicators are reported in 2021 international dollars (USD) adjusted for purchasing power parity. Joinpoint regression characterized 2000 to 2023 trends. RESULTS: From 2000 to 2023, total YLDs increased from 2367.81 (95% uncertainty interval [UI], 1067.67-4969.59) to 2941.68 (95% UI, 1252.99-6816.95) per 100 000 population, while economic losses increased from $80.10 billion (95% UI, $59.60-$104.69 billion) to $363.25 billion (95% UI, $264.04-$502.74 billion). papers.title: Development and Validation of the 9-item Parkinson's Disease Screening Questionnaire.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: We aimed to develop and validate a brief, self-administered questionnaire integrating motor and prodromal non-motor symptoms for screening Parkinson's disease (PD). METHODS: We conducted a three-phase study. Phase 1 used a prospectively registered systematic review of 107 studies to generate a 52-item draft. In Phase 2, the draft was refined in 205 participants (122 with early PD and 83 healthy controls) using item-level areas under the receiver operating characteristic curves (AUCs) and age- and sex-adjusted multivariable logistic regression. Phase 3 validated the 9-item Korean PD Screening Questionnaire (KPDSQ) in an independent cohort (n = 246; 122 PD, 45 essential tremor [ET], and 79 controls), and included a 4-week test-retest reassessment. RESULTS: The final 9-item KPDSQ comprises seven motor items (rest tremor, shuffling or short-step gait, slow daily activities, decreased arm swing, soft voice, masked face, and freezing of gait) and two non-motor items (hyposmia and dream-enactment behavior). At a cutoff of ≥2, sensitivity was 88.5% and specificity was 92.4% for distinguishing PD from controls (AUC = 0.970; 95% CI, 0.946-0.984; p < 0.001). At ≥3, the KPDSQ distinguished PD from ET (AUC = 0.774; 95% CI, 0.680-0.847; p < 0.001). Internal consistency was high (Cronbach's α = 0.800), test-retest reliability was excellent (ICC = 0.921), and scores correlated with MDS-UPDRS Part III scores in patients with PD (Spearman's ρ = 0.330; p < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: The 9-item KPDSQ is a reliable, clinically valid screening tool combining motor and prodromal non-motor features. Prospective community-based validation is warranted.

papers.title: Deep brain stimulation as neuroimmune-metabolic modulation in Parkinson's disease and beyond: tissue response, glial remodeling, and disease modification.
papers.abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is an established symptomatic therapy for Parkinson's disease (PD), yet its biological effects extend beyond modulation of abnormal basal ganglia circuitry. This review conceptualizes DBS in PD as a neuroimmune-metabolic intervention acting across the electrode-tissue interface, glial networks, peripheral immunity, and activity-dependent metabolic systems. PD is characterized by convergent immune and metabolic vulnerability. These processes create a disease environment in which electrical stimulation may interact with inflammation, excitotoxicity, bioenergetic stress, and neuronal resilience. We distinguish implantation-related tissue responses from stimulation-induced biological remodeling. Electrode insertion produces acute injury, blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, peri-electrode edema, gliosis, and foreign-body responses, which should not be conflated with the effects of chronic stimulation. Active DBS may modulate central cytokine expression, microglial and astrocytic phenotypes, inflammasome activity, astrocytic glutamate transport, and brain-peripheral immune crosstalk. Emerging evidence also suggests a neurometabolic dimension, including changes in regional glucose utilization, PD-related metabolic network expression, oxidative stress, and neurotrophic signaling. However, these effects are context-dependent and influenced by multiple factors. Although preclinical studies support potential neuroprotective mechanisms involving BDNF/TrkB signaling, mitophagy, reduced excitotoxic-inflammatory coupling, and immune-metabolic rebalancing, clinical evidence remains insufficient to establish DBS as a disease-modifying therapy. Future studies should integrate multiple methods such as longitudinal imaging, electrophysiology, immune profiling and metabolomics. DBS should be understood as a symptomatic circuit-based therapy that may also interact with neuroimmune and metabolic processes, while current evidence remains insufficient to estab

papers.title: Gait characteristics in people with central nervous system disorders under dual-task experimental paradigms: a scoping review.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Dual-task (DT) paradigms are widely used for gait assessment in patients with central nervous system diseases. However, previous studies have primarily focused on specific diseases and a limited range of DT paradigms, making it difficult to obtain an overall understanding of the application patterns of different paradigms and their associated gait changes. This scoping review aimed to identify and classify the DT paradigms used in DT gait studies of Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and stroke; describe the application and distribution of these paradigms across studies of different diseases; further examine changes in gait characteristics under different DT paradigms. METHODS: The Web of Science Core Collection, PubMed, and the Cochrane Library were systematically searched for relevant studies published between January 1, 2005, and April 30, 2026. DT paradigms were classified, and their distribution was mapped by disease category. Dual-task cost (DTC) for gait speed, stride length, and cadence was also summarized descriptively. RESULTS: A total of 84 studies were included, and 26 DT paradigms were identified, including 21 cognitive tasks, four motor tasks, and one combined cognitive-motor task. Serial subtraction by 3s and 7s were more frequently used in studies of PD, whereas the counting task was more frequently used in studies of AD. The verbal fluency task was relatively evenly distributed across studies of the three diseases, whereas the object-carrying task was used primarily in studies of PD and stroke. Among the paradigms included in the descriptive synthesis, mean gait speed DTC was numerically highest under the verbal fluency task in patients with AD, under serial subtraction by 7s in patients with PD and healthy controls, and under the counting task in patients with stroke. papers.title: Correlation Between Cognitive Function and Serum Irisin Levels in Parkinson's Disease Patients.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Cognitive impairment is a common non-motor symptom of Parkinson's disease (PD) that markedly reduces patients' quality of life. Given the clinical heterogeneity of PD-related cognitive impairment (PDCI), further clarification of clinical and circulating biological factors associated with cognitive status may help improve our understanding of cognitive dysfunction in PD. METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, 243 patients with PD and 90 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HCs) were enrolled. Cognitive function was evaluated using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), and patients with PD were classified into the PD with cognitive impairment (PDCI) and PD without cognitive impairment (PDNCI) groups. Based on motor symptoms, PD patients were further divided into three subtypes: tremor-dominant (TD), postural instability and gait disorder (PIGD), and indeterminate subtype (IND). Group comparisons and logistic regression analyses were performed to examine factors associated with cognitive impairment. RESULTS: Serum irisin levels did not differ significantly between patients with PD and healthy controls (p = 0.478). Compared with PDNCI patients, those with PDCI had lower serum irisin levels. Among motor subtypes, the PIGD group showed a higher prevalence of cognitive impairment (68.8% vs. 46.2%, p < 0.001) and significantly lower irisin levels compared with the TD group [3.25 (2.62-4.14) vs. 4.12 (3.42-5.07) µg/mL, p < 0.001]. Serum irisin levels were weakly but positively associated with memory performance, and this association remained significant after FDR correction across the five cognitive domains (r = 0.194, FDR-adjusted p = 0.010). Compared with patients in the TD-high irisin group, those in the PIGD-low irisin group had higher odds of concurrent cognitive impairment (OR = 6.065, 95% CI: 2.974-18.638, p = 0.002). papers.title: Determinants of Cueing Responsiveness in Parkinson's Disease: Insights from the UNITE-PD Study.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cueing strategies are widely used to improve gait in Parkinson's disease (PD), but interindividual variability in cueing responsiveness remains poorly understood. OBJECTIVES: The objective of the study was to identify determinants of internal and external cueing efficacy in persons with PD. METHODS: We performed a multicenter cohort study within the UNITE-PD consortium, including 277 persons with PD and self-reported gait impairment. Participants underwent motor, cognitive, and affective status assessments, followed by gait evaluations during uncued walking, external cueing (metronome), and internal cueing (silent counting). The dependent variable was cueing efficacy, expressed as change in stride time variability relative to uncued gait. Univariable and multivariable regression analyses, bootstrap resampling, and principal axis factoring were performed separately for internal and external cueing. RESULTS: Cueing efficacy for both external and internal cueing was greater in persons with higher uncued stride time variability. Bootstrap analyses showed inconsistent selection of individual clinical tests. Factor analysis identified motor and cognitive constructs associated with cueing efficacy for both cueing types, with affective status additionally contributing to internal cueing responsiveness. A significant three-way interaction between stride time variability, motor performance, and cognitive performance was found for internal cueing responsiveness. CONCLUSIONS: Cueing efficacy in PD is governed by uncued gait impairment at baseline and the interplay of motor, cognitive, and affective capacities, rather than by isolated clinical measures. These findings support the concept that cueing responsiveness depends on the availability and recruitment of strategy-specific (sub-)cerebral resources across motor, cognitive, and affective domains, where preserved capacity in one domain seems to offset limitations in another. © 2026 The Author(s). papers.title: Research Progress of Low-Intensity Pulsed Ultrasound in Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder where current pharmacological and surgical interventions, including Deep Brain Stimulation, often fail to reverse neuronal degeneration or halt disease progression. Low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS) has emerged as a novel, non-invasive neuromodulation technology with significant therapeutic potential. This review synthesizes current research on the key acoustic parameters, biological mechanisms, and clinical applications of LIPUS in PD. Unlike High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound (HIFU), which relies on thermal ablation to destroy target nuclei (e.g., Vim, STN), LIPUS utilizes low-energy mechanical waves (typically <3 W/cm²) to exert non-thermal regulatory effects without damaging tissue. Mechanisms of action include the modulation of mechanosensitive ion channels (e.g., Piezo1), enhancement of neuroplasticity via brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), promotion of autophagy, and regulation of microglial phenotypes to reduce neuroinflammation. We further compare LIPUS with HIFU, highlighting the superiority of LIPUS regarding safety, reversibility, and the absence of requirement for MRI-based thermal monitoring. While preliminary clinical studies using wearable LIPUS devices indicate improvements in motor and cognitive functions, a unified consensus on optimal stimulation parameters and targeting strategies is lacking. Future research should focus on large-scale, standardized clinical trials to establish precise protocols for LIPUS as a disease-modifying therapy for PD.

papers.title: Case Report: Metabolic adaptations to intensive aerobic training in Parkinson's disease: autonomic and physiopathological response.
papers.journal: Frontiers in sports and active living
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Aerobic exercise is a key non-pharmacological intervention in Parkinson's disease (PD), yet the physiological mechanisms underlying its therapeutic effects remain incompletely understood. This case report aimed to investigate metabolic and cardiovascular adaptations to an intensive aerobic training programme in a person with PD, with particular focus on metabolic efficiency and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) response. METHODS: A 72-year-old man with idiopathic PD (Hoehn & Yahr stage II, ON medication) participated in a 4-week intensive treadmill training programme (20 sessions) within the METEX-PD protocol. Exercise was performed at a constant external workload (5.0-5.5 km·h⁻1 RESULTS: Progressive reductions in HR,    V DISCUSSION: Intensive aerobic training induced favourable metabolic adaptations in this individual with PD, as evidenced by improved aerobic efficiency and increased circulating IGF-1 levels. These adaptations occurred despite potential autonomic dysfunction affecting cardiovascular responses. The findings support the use of direct metabolic measurements to better characterise training adaptations and optimise individualised aerobic exercise prescription in people with PD. Further studies are warranted to confirm these observations in larger cohorts.

papers.title: Hearing Loss and Parkinson's Disease: Insights From Human and Animal Studies.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hearing loss (HL) has been increasingly implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD), but the epidemiological association between them and the underlying biological mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the association between HL and PD and to explore potential biological links between auditory deprivation and PD-related pathology. METHODS: Data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) and the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) were analyzed using multivariable logistic regression, with sensitivity analyses performed in propensity score-matched samples comprising 70 matched pairs in NHANES and 171 matched pairs in CHARLS. In parallel, an auditory-deprivation model was established by ossicular chain interruption, while PD-related pathology was modeled by MPTP administration once daily in three 7-day treatment blocks (21 injections in total), with 48-h drug-free assessment intervals between blocks. Auditory deprivation was confirmed by auditory brainstem response. Motor function was assessed using the open field and rotarod tests, and dopaminergic neuron loss was evaluated by immunofluorescence. Striatal RNA sequencing, integrated with the GSE205450 dataset, was conducted to explore potential molecular mechanisms. RESULTS: Self-reported hearing impairment was associated with higher odds of PD in both NHANES (OR, 1.79; 95% CI, 1.24-2.58) and CHARLS (OR, 1.42; 95% CI, 1.01-2.01). In propensity score-matched analyses, the association remained significant in NHANES (70 matched pairs) and CHARLS (171 matched pairs). In animal experiments, significant HL × MPTP interactions were observed for motor performance and TH-positive dopaminergic neuron counts, with poorer outcomes in HL + MPTP mice than in MPTP-only mice. papers.title: Caregiver Contributions to Self-Care in Parkinson's Disease: A Qualitative Descriptive Study.
papers.journal: Journal of nursing scholarship : an official publication of Sigma Theta Tau International Honor Society of Nursing
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder after Alzheimer's disease, and is characterized by motor symptoms such as bradykinesia, rigidity, and reduced movement automaticity. Caregiver contributions (CC) to self-care in PD represent an important resource for supporting people with PD. However, this topic has not yet been fully explored. AIM: To explore CC to self-care in PD across the domains of CC to self-care maintenance, monitoring, and management. METHOD: A qualitative study design was conducted using a combined deductive and inductive approach. An initial deductive framework guided the analysis, while an inductive process allowed the identification of additional codes emerging from the interview data. RESULTS: Twenty semi-structured interviews were conducted. Caregivers of people with PD were 75% women, with a mean age of 63.7 years, and were 90% spouses and 95% living with the patient. The analysis showed that the CC to self-care emerges across all domains: in self-care maintenance, through support for medication adherence, physical activity, safety, and diet; in self-care monitoring, through support in daily activities, routine symptom monitoring, and alert system monitoring; and in self-care management, through symptom management strategies and caregiver attitudes. More broadly, this contribution also emerged in relation to caregiving difficulties, interactions with healthcare professionals, and the information that guides self-care. DISCUSSION-CONCLUSION: The findings from this study showed that caregivers of persons with PD play a significant role in CC to self-care maintenance, monitoring, and management, particularly through non-pharmacological strategies. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These data are fundamental for guiding educational interventions aimed at the caregivers of patients with PD.

papers.title: Initiating levodopa pump therapy: a qualitative study of patient and caregiver perspectives.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder affecting motor and non-motor functions. When oral medication no longer provides adequate control, device-aided therapies (DAT), including levodopa infusion therapy, may be introduced. Although DAT can improve symptom management, little is known about how people with PD (PwPD) and family caregivers (FC) experience the initiation process. This study explored PwPD and their FC perceptions during decision-making, therapy initiation, and subsequent adaptation to levodopa pump therapy. METHODS: This qualitative study employed semi-structured interviews (6-24 months after treatment initiation) and latent reflexive thematic analysis with ten PwPD and nine FC recruited from two Swedish university hospitals. RESULTS: Thematic analysis revealed four shared themes: (1) Living with the constraints of PD, (2) Sustaining hope in the face of therapeutic uncertainty, (3) Adapting to a new treatment while facing practical challenges, and (4) Relying on expertise while managing its absence. Pump therapy was often chosen due to limited alternatives and strong trust in the specialized multidisciplinary PD team. While both groups experienced symptom improvements, PwPD focused on autonomy whereas FC focused on responsibilities. Expectations were generally met, yet FC frequently felt underinformed about the realities of daily pump management. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings highlight that although symptom control improved, both PwPD and FC continued to face practical and emotional challenges. Supporting their adaptation process requires coordinated, person-centred preparation, guidance and follow-up from multidisciplinary, specialized PD teams. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: Not applicable.

papers.title: Morning lighting intervention reduces fatigue and improves sleep in Parkinson disease.
papers.journal: Neurotherapeutics : the journal of the American Society for Experimental NeuroTherapeutics
papers.abstract: Fatigue and sleep disturbances are common in Parkinson Disease (PD) and significantly reduce quality of life, yet effective pharmacological treatments are limited. Light therapy offers a promising non-pharmacologic approach, but most lighting interventions have focused on improving sleep. Using a novel and easily administered morning lighting intervention, we previously demonstrated improvement in sleep duration. We have now extended the prior study through the addition of 23 individuals to investigate the intervention's effect on fatigue and sleep. In this single-arm intervention study, participants received morning light for 4 consecutive weeks from table or floor luminaires designed to deliver circadian-effective ambient light at home. Objective sleep was measured with wrist-worn actigraphy and subjective sleep, fatigue and mood were assessed using standardized questionnaires. Analysis of pre and post intervention data for the current cohort was performed separately as well as in combination with the 20 participants from the previously reported pilot study. For the 23 current participants, fatigue on the Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy-Fatigue (FACIT-F) scale improved by 3.9 ± 1.00 points (p = 0.0026). While sleep duration increased by mean 21.3 ± 14.4 min, it was not statistically significant (p = 0.082). When combined with the 20 participants from the prior pilot study, significant improvement in fatigue by 2.8 ± 0.85 points (p = 0.0033) was observed and sleep duration was also significantly increased by 24.7 ± 10.4 min (p = 0.012). These findings support morning light as a novel intervention for fatigue in PD.

papers.title: Upregulation of ZBTB20 indirectly participate in ferroptosis of Parkinson's disease by neuronal glial interactions.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's Disease (PD) is an age- associated late-onset neurodegenerative disorder characterized by typical dysfunction and diverse non-motor complications, which severely impair the quality of life of elderly patients. The present study systematically investigated the biological function, diagnostic value, and underlying molecular mechanisms of zinc finger and BTB domain-containing 20 (ZBTB20) in the pathological progression of PD. Both transcriptional and translational analyses demonstrated significant upregulation of ZBTB20 expression in in vivo PD mouse models and in vitro PD cellular models. Functional cellular experiments revealed that ZBTB20 overexpression markedly promoted mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation and aggravated oxidative stress in PD cell lines, whereas ZBTB20 knockdown exerted the opposite protective effects. Consistent with the in vitro observations, in vivo striatal injection of sh-ZBTB20 effectively alleviated pathological lesions and mitigated ROS-mediated oxidative damage in PD mice. Further mechanistic validation from in vitro and in vivo experiments confirmed that ZBTB20 upregulation facilitates ferroptosis during PD progression. Notably, pharmacological activation of ferroptosis completely abolished the motor protective phenotypes induced by ZBTB20 silencing in PD mice, verifying the critical involvement of ferroptosis in ZBTB20-mediated PD pathogenesis. Mechanistic exploration revealed that ZBTB20 knockdown significantly elevated the protein abundance of large tumor suppressor kinase 1 (LATS1) in PD models. Co-immunoprecipitation assays further validated a direct physical interaction between ZBTB20 and LATS1. Specifically, ZBTB20 promotes LATS1 ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation in vitro. Moreover, pharmacological inhibition of LATS1 effectively reversed the inhibitory effect of ZBTB20 knockdown on microglial ferroptosis in PD models. papers.title: Family and community care for older persons with Parkinson's disease in Kenya: a qualitative, ethnographic study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Informal family care remains central to care for older adults in Kenya, yet evidence hints towards an 'erosion' of large, multi-generational family care networks and a conditionality on reciprocity across many African countries. The increasing incidence and prevalence of chronic conditions associated with later life have made care needs more complex and resource intensive. Parkinson's is one such example of a progressive condition characterised by a host of motor and non-motor symptoms, which results in increasing disability over time and, therefore, care requirements and resources. The experience of older persons experiencing progressive disability, and the impact on family care, is under-reported in Kenya and across Africa. METHODS: This paper reports an ethnographic study on the lived experiences of older persons with Parkinson's (aged 60 and older) and their families living in urban and rural Kenya, drawing on interview material and observations involving 45 people with Parkinson's and 23 family caregivers to explore the experiences of receiving and providing care. RESULTS: The paper explores care provision and receipt in the context of ageing with Parkinson's as a progressive movement disorder, demonstrating the resilience and adaptability of older adults and their caregivers. Structural, cultural and community processes situate the individual experiences of PwP and family caregivers, who navigate taboos and tensions in reciprocity and resources to make care work. These experiences have implications for who takes on the caring role, and the resulting adaptations, reconfigurations and emerging forms of care that families enact, including unconventional co-residence. papers.title: Evaluating the NLRP3 inflammasome in chemotherapy-induced cognitive impairment: A multi-timepoint study of methotrexate and 5-fluorouracil in female rats.
papers.abstract: Chemotherapy-induced cognitive impairment (CICI) affects many cancer survivors, who often report cognitive difficulties during and/or after treatment that reduce quality of life. While the exact mechanisms that underlie CICI are unclear, neuroinflammation is widely proposed to contribute. One candidate mediator is the nucleotide-binding domain leucine-rich repeat and pyrin domain containing receptor protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome, which drives microglial inflammation and is implicated in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease. This study therefore investigated whether NLRP3 inflammasome components are altered in a rat model of CICI. Female Sprague Dawley rats were randomly allocated to receive methotrexate (MTX), 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) or saline (n = 18/treatment) and were euthanised at 96-hours, 31-days or 93-days post-treatment (n = 6/treatment/timepoint). This cohort was previously shown to develop cognitive deficits. In the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus, NLRP3 and pro-caspase-1 were measured by western blot, and interleukin-1β (IL-1β) by ELISA. Microglial number and activation were assessed by ionized calcium-binding adaptor molecule 1 (IBA1) immunohistochemistry (n = 4/treatment/timepoint). Compared with saline controls, neither chemotherapy altered NLRP3 or pro-caspase-1 in either brain region at any timepoint, and treatment effect sizes were small (ηp² ≤ 0.06). IL-1β, detectable only at 96-hours, was also unchanged. Similarly, there were no differences in either total microglial number or the percentage of activated microglia. These findings provide no evidence that NLRP3 inflammasome components are altered in this female rat model of CICI at the timepoints examined. However, as inflammasome assembly and activation were not directly assessed, future work should measure ASC speck formation, cleaved caspase-1 and mature IL-1β, and include earlier timepoints, particularly within the first two weeks after chemotherapy.
